question.problem:
For the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

$$
f(x,y)=(x-y)^{3},
$$

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-6 & ∗ \\ 6 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ ∗\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the sum of the three missing expressions.

current_example.problem:
For the function $f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R,$ defined as

$$
f\left(x,y \right) 
=
x^2y-xy^3,
$$

determine the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14197045/assets/a7dc6579f367779f98cd17ac764f23dd46d1b67d30a62585b8be7db44388b650.svg) Give your answer in matrix form.
current_example.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $\mathbf{f}:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ is defined by 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14197045/assets/0306b1681e4d013c50849e08d28a9da9c89289a12dc27322d3664926467f1e3b.svg) 

and is twice differentiable at $\mathbf x = \mathbf a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $\mathbf a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14197045/assets/2552f04c523794aefc14020b3330fa73c6aab95e18c84bf51a9a818dcd4f85f6.svg)

and

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14197045/assets/70f039d87eb91cef4aa6205ade74a29bc35b02439a485d71c8a1cabdf7f7175d.svg)

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial:

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2xy-{y}^{3} & {x}^{2}-3x{y}^{2}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{′}(1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2y & 2x-3{y}^{2} \\ 2x-3{y}^{2} & -6xy\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial (in matrix form) is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14197045/assets/fd2bf54e6c742921e1921b68606b1ce3eb583eb749795166d761abdef10aa7e9.svg)
